covers.quote: You don’t need a comma after an introductory word if the sentence is very short.

rules.quote: Use a comma after introductory words, such as greetings and adverbs, or when addressing someone.
rules.specification: Treat “very short” as 4 or fewer words.
rules.violation_condition: An introductory word is not followed by a comma, except in a sentence of 4 or fewer words.
when: Do not require the comma after an introductory word in a sentence of 4 or fewer words.
rules.why: One check for commas after introductory words; the short-sentence exception changes when it applies, not the rule (G-2, G-3).

covers.quote: Conditional clauses are adverbial clauses (for example, beginning with ‘if’, ‘unless’ or ‘until’). They should also have a comma after them if they start the sentence.

rules.quote: Use commas after adverbial phrases and adverbial clauses.
rules.violation_condition: An introductory adverbial phrase or clause is not followed by a comma.
when: The phrase or clause is introductory. If it is moved to the end of the sentence, do not add a comma before it.
rules.why: This is a specific introductory-phrase-and-clause rule; the conditional-clause instruction is a case of the same check (G-1, G-2).

covers.quote: Use a comma after an introductory phrase that ends with a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral.
Avoid this type of sentence structure because the string of numbers can be confusing.

rules.quote: Avoid beginning a sentence with a string of numbers and dates
rules.specification: The construction described on this page is a sentence beginning with an introductory phrase that ends in a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence begins with an introductory phrase ending in a numeral, immediately followed by another numeral.
rules.why: The heading states a text-structure rule, while the body narrows the construction it concerns (G-4).

rules.quote: Use a comma after an introductory phrase that ends with a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral.
rules.violation_condition: An introductory phrase ending with a numeral is immediately followed by another numeral without a comma after the phrase.
when: The rule applies regardless of how short the sentence is.
rules.why: This is a distinct punctuation check from avoiding the sentence structure: a sentence can use this comma and still be discouraged by the separate structure rule.

covers.quote: Don’t use commas if the clause is essential for meaning.
If you can remove the clause and your sentence means the same thing, it’s non-essential and should go between commas.
Within a sentence, use a pair of commas to separate non-essential or supplementary information.
Generally, if you can take out part of the sentence and it is still grammatically correct, it should be between a pair of commas.
Always check for the second comma where there should be a pair.

rules.quote: Use commas around clauses that add information but aren’t essential to the meaning of the sentence.
rules.violation_condition: A non-essential clause is not set off with a pair of commas.
when: Use commas only when the clause is non-essential. A clause is non-essential if removing it leaves the sentence with the same meaning.
rules.why: The clause-specific rule is retained; the essential-clause instruction and removal test describe when the same comma check applies (G-1, G-2).

covers.quote: You should be able to take out the noun phrase between the comma pair and still have a grammatically correct sentence.
Within a sentence, use a pair of commas to separate non-essential or supplementary information.
Generally, if you can take out part of the sentence and it is still grammatically correct, it should be between a pair of commas.
Always check for the second comma where there should be a pair.

rules.quote: Use a pair of commas when you have 2 noun phrases next to each other that define the same thing.
rules.violation_condition: Two adjacent noun phrases define the same thing, but the supplementary phrase is not set off with a pair of commas.
when: The two adjacent noun phrases define the same thing, and the second phrase is supplementary rather than essential to identifying it.
rules.why: This is the specific rule for supplementary noun phrases; the take-out test and general paired-comma guidance are restatements (G-1, G-2, G-4).

rules.quote: Use a comma before a question that is part of the sentence.
rules.violation_condition: A question tagged onto the end of a sentence is not preceded by a comma.
when: The question is tagged onto the end of a sentence.
rules.why: Question tags are a distinct punctuation case retained as their own rule (G-1).

covers.quote: If ‘for example’ begins a sentence, it is an introductory phrase. Follow it with a comma.

rules.quote: Generally, use a comma before and after the phrase ‘for example’ in a sentence.
rules.violation_condition: The phrase ‘for example’ in a sentence is missing a required comma before or after it.
when: When ‘for example’ begins a sentence, follow it with a comma rather than requiring a comma before it.
rules.why: The in-sentence and sentence-initial placements are conditions for the comma rule; the bullet-list colon is a separate punctuation check (G-2).

rules.quote: If you’re introducing a bullet list after ‘for example’, use a colon.
rules.violation_condition: A bullet list introduced after ‘for example’ is not preceded by a colon.
when: ‘For example’ introduces a bullet list.
rules.why: The colon before a bullet list is a distinct check from comma placement around the phrase in a sentence.

rules.quote: If you use Latin shortened forms, such as ‘e.g.’ and ‘i.e.’, don’t follow them with a comma.
rules.violation_condition: A comma follows a Latin shortened form such as ‘e.g.’ or ‘i.e.’.
when: The Latin shortened form is used.
rules.why: This is a distinct punctuation rule with a recognizable word-and-punctuation pattern.

covers.quote: If they have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.
If 2 clauses share the same subject, you don’t need to repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction.
The exception to this rule is when you have joined more than 2 principal clauses with the same subject.

rules.quote: Use commas to connect 2 or more principal clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’, ‘so’).
rules.violation_condition: Principal clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction are missing a comma in a case where the comma is required.

when: The quotation ends the sentence.
rules.why: This is a distinct rule about retaining the original punctuation when a quotation ends the sentence.
